messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Combat Engineer
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Fire/Flames): Fire or flames, Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Shouting: Shouting
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marisol is a 54-year-old Latina combat engineer who came to treatment after years of trying to keep herself tightly controlled at work and at home. She has been married for decades and still speaks about the military with pride, but when she describes the deployment that stays with her, her account breaks apart into sensory fragments rather than a single narrative. She can say where she was assigned and that her unit was working around damaged roads and explosives, but when she tries to explain what happened on the day that most haunts her, she loses the sequence. What remains immediate to her are flashes and bodily impressions: the sudden sight of fire, the feel of intense heat striking her skin, men shouting over one another, and the sense that everything had turned dangerous in an instant.

She remembers being in the middle of a mission environment that had already taught her to expect hidden threat. Then came a blast-related incident she still cannot recount cleanly from beginning to end. She recalls flames rising fast enough that they seemed to swallow the scene, the heat on her face and arms, and the voices around her turning into shouted commands and panic. Even now, when the memory comes, she does not first think it through as a past event. She hears it. In her mind there are the same shouted words and urgent tones from that moment, as if the sound has returned before she has any chance to prepare herself. She says it can happen “out of nowhere,” with something in her surroundings pulling the whole thing back in an instant before she even realizes she has been triggered.

After she returned, the world did not feel ordinary again. Marisol had come to believe that danger was not exceptional but everywhere, waiting behind appearances. She noticed that her body rarely settled; she stayed tense, shoulders tight, muscles braced, as if she might need to react at any second. Silence became almost as unsettling as noise. If a room, a street, or a worksite went unusually quiet, she felt a rush of certainty that something bad was about to happen. In those moments she would start scanning automatically—doorways, corners, who was standing where, what could ignite, what did not look right. As a combat engineer she is often in environments where alertness is part of the culture, and that made it easy for this constant checking to blend into her work life. But coworkers noticed that she was doing more than being careful. If a training area was too still, or if someone suddenly raised their voice across the site, Marisol’s attention would snap away from the task in front of her. She struggled to concentrate and sometimes had to ask for instructions to be repeated because her mind had already shifted to searching for threat.

Certain moments in daily life became especially hard to manage. A burst of flames from a grill, the sight of a controlled burn, or even heat from machinery hitting her skin in a particular way could bring back the whole scene so fast it felt as though past and present had collapsed together. Shouting was particularly potent. At work, if supervisors or crew members called out loudly over equipment noise, she could feel her body surge before she had time to think. At home, even raised voices from a television in another room could leave her withdrawn and on edge. She found she could not tell herself a coherent story afterward; she only knew that she had been back there again.

Over the months and years, Marisol shaped her life around reducing strain. She began avoiding anything she thought might be stressful, not because she saw herself as fragile but because she believed pressure made everything harder to contain. She turned down situations that felt unpredictable, kept her routines narrow, and tried not to engage emotionally with things that might stir her up. She describes this as numbing herself, flattening her feelings so she could get through the day. Her husband experienced her as increasingly distant. She was physically present but hard to reach, and when he asked what was wrong she often said she did not know how to explain it.

Alongside this was a harsh private view of herself. Marisol had come to believe there was something wrong with her as a person because she still reacted this way after so many years. She also returned again and again to the conviction that what happened was profoundly unfair and that nothing meaningful had ever been done about it. That sense of injustice sat beside her broader belief that the world is dangerous, that safety is temporary at best and never to be trusted.

She sought help only recently, after noticing that her concentration at work had become harder to hide and that her life had narrowed to managing the next reaction. What finally brought her in was not one dramatic crisis but the accumulation of too many moments when flames, heat on her skin, or someone shouting transported her without warning. She says she is tired of living as if danger is always just about to break through the silence. What frightens her most is the idea that this is simply who she is now; what she hopes, cautiously, is that she might one day be able to remember what happened without feeling as if it is happening again.
